title: Three Meals a Day: Rethinking Welfare for the World's Delivery Riders
author: AztutMind
summary: A global proposal for a more humane delivery economy: providing qualifying delivery workers with three nutritious meals, hydration and rest support without reducing their wages.
content:
A Global Proposal for a More Humane Delivery Economy

Every day, millions of people around the world order food through digital platforms.

A few taps on a phone can bring a meal from a restaurant to a home, office, hotel or workplace.

Behind that extraordinary convenience is another system that is much less visible:

the delivery worker.

The rider who collects the food.

The rider who travels through traffic.

The rider who waits outside restaurants.

The rider who searches for buildings.

The rider who carries the order to the customer's door.

The rider who continues to the next order.

And then the next.

And the next.

The global online food-delivery economy has become enormous. One recent estimate places global online food-delivery activity at around 32.1 billion orders in 2025, equivalent to approximately 88 million orders per day. Because different research firms define and measure "food delivery" differently, this should be understood as an industry estimate rather than an exact global count.

Other research shows just how deeply delivery has entered everyday life: more than three billion people worldwide use online food-delivery services, according to Statista's current global overview.

At this scale, an important question deserves attention:

Who takes care of the person delivering the food?

The Proposal

Three Meals a Day

The basic idea is simple:

Every delivery worker completing a qualifying full-day shift should have access to three nutritious meals at no cost to their wages.

Breakfast

Before or near the beginning of the working period.

Lunch

During the main working period.

Dinner

For workers whose shifts extend into the evening.

The benefit should be:

Food — not cash.

Because the objective is not merely to increase income.

The objective is to make sure that a person doing demanding work actually has access to food.

1. Why a Cash Allowance May Not Be Enough

Imagine that a company gives a rider a daily food allowance.

It sounds generous.

But the worker may think:

"I can save this money."

Why?

Because the money may be more valuable to the worker's family than it is to the worker personally.

A rider may have:

  • children;
  • parents;
  • a spouse;
  • education expenses;
  • household bills;
  • debt;
  • medical expenses;
  • family members depending on their income.

So the worker may skip breakfast.

Then skip lunch.

Then eat something very inexpensive at night.

The money is saved.

The family benefits.

But the worker has sacrificed his own nutrition.

This is not necessarily because the worker is irresponsible.

It may be because the worker is responsible for other people.

That is precisely why a food allowance and a food benefit are not the same thing.

2. Salary Belongs to the Worker

This proposal should never interfere with wages.

A worker's earnings should remain completely his or her own.

The worker should be free to:

  • spend them;
  • save them;
  • send them to family;
  • invest them;
  • use them for any legitimate personal purpose.

The three meals are an additional workplace benefit.

Therefore:

Salary
The worker's money.

Three meals
The employer/platform welfare benefit.

That distinction is fundamental.

3. Why Three Meals?

If someone is working a full-day shift, providing only one meal may not address the entire problem.

Consider a worker beginning early in the morning and finishing late in the evening.

He or she may need:

Breakfast → Lunch → Dinner

Just as many conventional workplaces provide access to meals, cafeterias, meal subsidies or food facilities, mobile workers deserve an equivalent form of support.

The difference is that a delivery rider doesn't necessarily have a permanent workplace cafeteria.

Their workplace is the road.

Therefore, the meal must travel with the job.

4. The Road Is Their Workplace

For an office employee:

Workplace → Desk → Cafeteria → Meal

For a delivery worker:

Workplace → Road → Restaurant → Road → Customer → Road

The worker is constantly moving.

That makes conventional employee welfare models difficult to apply.

A rider may not have:

  • a staff cafeteria;
  • a fixed lunchroom;
  • a company kitchen;
  • a predictable meal location.

The solution therefore needs to be digital and distributed.

5. The Digital Meal Wallet

Every eligible rider could receive a Digital Meal Wallet inside the delivery app.

The wallet could show:

Today's Benefits

  • 🍳 Breakfast — Available
  • 🍛 Lunch — Available
  • 🍲 Dinner — Available

The rider selects a meal from participating restaurants.

A QR code is generated.

The restaurant scans the code.

The meal is provided.

The transaction is recorded automatically.

There is no need for:

  • cash reimbursement;
  • paper coupons;
  • expense claims;
  • salary deductions.

6. Give Workers Choice

A global programme cannot assume everyone eats the same food.

The rider should have choices.

Vegetarian Meals

  • rice + lentils + vegetables;
  • chapati + curry;
  • vegetable rice;
  • paneer meal;
  • vegetable noodles.

Non-Vegetarian Meals

  • chicken + rice;
  • chicken curry + bread;
  • fish meal;
  • egg meal;
  • chicken noodles.

Breakfast

  • eggs + bread;
  • porridge;
  • dosa/idli;
  • breakfast sandwich;
  • yoghurt + fruit.

Light Meals

  • sandwich;
  • wrap;
  • salad + protein;
  • yoghurt + fruit.

The company provides the entitlement.

The worker chooses the food.

7. Three Meals Should Not Mean Three Identical Meals

The programme could encourage variety.

Breakfast

Protein + carbohydrate + fruit

Lunch

Protein + vegetables + carbohydrate

Dinner

Balanced meal + hydration

The goal is not luxury.

The goal is:

Reliable access to reasonably nutritious food during a demanding working day.

8. Water Should Be Part of the Benefit

Food alone isn't enough.

A delivery worker may spend hours travelling outdoors or working in difficult environmental conditions.

Therefore:

Three Meals + Hydration

could become the basic package.

Participating locations could provide:

  • drinking water;
  • appropriate beverages;
  • electrolyte support where justified;
  • seating;
  • rest areas.

The welfare programme could therefore become:

Food + Water + Rest

rather than simply a food coupon.

9. The Programme Should Not Encourage Excessive Working

There is an important safeguard.

A company should not create:

"Work longer → receive more food."

That could unintentionally encourage excessive working hours.

Instead, eligibility could be based on reasonable working periods.

For example:

Short shift → Appropriate meal entitlement

Standard full-day shift → Three meals

Extended shift → Additional welfare/hydration support where appropriate

The objective is worker wellbeing, not increasing hours.

10. Restaurants Become Partners

The programme doesn't require companies to build thousands of kitchens.

Existing restaurants can participate.

Imagine a network called:

Rider Meal Partners

Restaurants agree to provide approved meals at negotiated rates.

Suppose a meal normally costs:

$8

A restaurant participating in a large-volume programme might agree to provide it for:

$5–6

The restaurant gains predictable volume.

The platform gains a scalable welfare system.

The worker receives food.

This creates a circular model.

11. The Restaurant Gets Something in Return

The programme isn't simply charity for restaurants either.

A participating restaurant receives:

  • guaranteed demand;
  • predictable meal volume;
  • additional visibility;
  • potential long-term partnership;
  • potentially reduced food waste.

Restaurants could even create dedicated:

Rider Meal Menus

These could be designed specifically around:

  • nutrition;
  • affordability;
  • speed of preparation;
  • portability;
  • food safety.

12. Food Waste Can Become Part of the Solution

There is another opportunity.

Restaurants frequently have food that is safe and suitable for consumption but cannot be sold normally because of timing, excess production or inventory planning.

A controlled programme could potentially redirect eligible surplus food into approved rider-meal channels, subject to local food-safety requirements.

Recent initiatives have already demonstrated the basic principle of combining food support with delivery-rider welfare. For example, meal-distribution programmes have provided riders with meals and water through partnerships involving food banks and delivery companies.

The difference would be turning occasional assistance into a structured everyday welfare system.

13. The Global Delivery Economy Makes This Scalable

This idea becomes particularly interesting because delivery is no longer a niche activity.

Recent research describes the online food-delivery industry as a major global sector involving tens of millions of workers.

If even a fraction of these workers participated in a structured meal programme, the potential social impact would be enormous.

Consider an illustrative scenario:

10 Million Participating Workers

× 3 meals

= 30 million meals per working day

Over 300 working days:

= 9 billion meals per year

That is not a prediction.

It is an illustration of what happens when a relatively simple employee benefit is applied at global scale.

14. What Would It Cost?

The economics need to be studied carefully.

Suppose the negotiated average meal cost were:

$4

Three meals:

$12 per worker per day

For an illustrative 10 million workers:

$120 million per day

That is a huge number.

But the entire point of a global programme would be to avoid placing the entire cost on one company.

The cost could potentially be shared through a combination of:

  • delivery platforms;
  • fleet operators;
  • participating restaurants;
  • corporate sponsors;
  • food manufacturers;
  • supermarkets;
  • ESG/social-impact programmes;
  • voluntary customer contributions;
  • food-waste partnerships.

Bulk purchasing could also reduce the average cost.

The exact economics would need to be tested market by market.

15. A Customer Could Optionally Contribute

Imagine an order screen containing:

“Add a Meal for a Rider”

$0.50
$1
$2
No thanks

Millions of small contributions could potentially finance a meaningful portion of a welfare programme.

But there is an important principle:

Customer donations should supplement the programme, not replace the company's responsibility.

The company should fund a baseline benefit.

Customer participation should be voluntary.

16. Companies Could Sponsor Meals

Corporations could also participate.

For example:

“Company X is sponsoring 500,000 rider meals this year.”

The programme could publish transparent impact metrics:

  • Meals funded: 500,000
  • Workers supported: 25,000
  • Restaurants participating: 800

That is much more tangible than a generic statement about corporate social responsibility.

17. The Benefit Should Never Become Charity Theatre

There is a danger that companies could turn the programme into marketing.

A few free meals.

A photograph.

A press release.

Then the programme disappears.

That is not enough.

A serious programme should be:

Permanent

Not just during festivals or special events.

Measurable

The number of meals should be tracked.

Accessible

Workers should actually be able to redeem them.

Nutritious

The cheapest food shouldn't automatically qualify.

Voluntary

Workers choose what they eat.

Additional

The benefit should not replace wages.

18. Existing Initiatives Show That the Concept Is Feasible

This isn't an entirely theoretical idea.

Delivery companies and partner organisations already provide meals or food-related support to riders in different markets.

For example, Deliveroo has previously described a recurring programme in which restaurant partners provided riders with free meals and refreshments.

Other programmes have provided grocery kits or meals to riders during particular periods.

And recent rider-support initiatives have provided meals and water at designated rest areas.

These examples demonstrate something important:

The infrastructure and willingness to provide food already exist.

The opportunity is to move from occasional support to a more systematic welfare standard.

19. Why This Matters Beyond Comfort

Food isn't simply a perk.

It can affect:

  • energy;
  • concentration;
  • physical wellbeing;
  • ability to work safely;
  • mood;
  • recovery;
  • overall quality of life.

This becomes particularly important for workers whose jobs involve prolonged travel and road exposure.

Recent research and worker-rights investigations have also highlighted nutritional concerns among some delivery riders. One 2026 investigation involving 108 interviewed riders reported that 15% described inadequate access to nutrition.

That does not mean every delivery worker experiences this problem.

But it demonstrates why food access should be treated as a genuine welfare issue rather than merely a perk.

20. The Psychological Benefit

There is another dimension that cannot easily be measured in dollars.

Imagine beginning a working day knowing:

“My breakfast is taken care of.”

Then:

“My lunch is taken care of.”

And later:

“I don't have to worry about dinner either.”

That can remove a significant amount of everyday financial anxiety.

The worker can use his earnings for the things he considers most important.

Perhaps:

  • school fees
  • parents
  • rent
  • savings
  • sending money home

The worker doesn't have to sacrifice his own food in order to fulfil those responsibilities.

21. The Principle Behind the Idea

The programme can be built around one sentence:

A worker should never have to choose between feeding himself and supporting his family.

That is the heart of the proposal.

The worker's salary remains his.

His family remains his priority.

And his meals are provided separately as part of the working environment.

22. From Rider Welfare to a Global Standard

The idea could eventually evolve into something broader:

The 3×3 Rider Welfare Standard

3 Meals

Breakfast
Lunch
Dinner

3 Essentials

Food
Water
Rest

The standard could eventually include additional requirements around:

  • safety;
  • reasonable working hours;
  • accident protection;
  • access to medical assistance;
  • appropriate rest;
  • fair employment arrangements.

The meal component could become the simplest starting point.

23. A Possible Certification

3×3 Rider Care Certified

designation.

To qualify, a company might need to demonstrate:

  • ✓ Three-meal access for qualifying full-day workers
  • ✓ Drinking-water access
  • ✓ Participating meal locations
  • ✓ Transparent redemption data
  • ✓ No salary deduction for meals
  • ✓ Nutritional standards
  • ✓ Worker feedback mechanisms
  • ✓ Safety and rest provisions

This could turn rider welfare into something customers can recognize.

Instead of simply asking:

“Which app delivers fastest?”

customers might eventually ask:

“Which company treats its delivery workers best?”

24. The Future of Food Delivery Should Include the Worker

Technology has transformed delivery.

Artificial intelligence can optimize routes.

Algorithms can assign orders.

GPS can track riders.

Apps can predict arrival times.

Restaurants can automate kitchens.

Customers can order with one tap.

But technology should not make the human being invisible.

The delivery worker remains the person physically carrying the meal from one place to another.

The future of delivery should therefore not only be:

Faster.

Cheaper.

More efficient.

It should also be:

More humane.

Conclusion

The world may process tens of millions of food-delivery orders every day.

Behind those orders are millions of people whose work makes that convenience possible.

A food allowance is useful.

But an allowance can be saved.

A discount is useful.

But a discount doesn't guarantee that a worker will eat.

A special meal campaign is valuable.

But temporary programmes cannot solve a permanent welfare need.

The more ambitious idea is:

Three Meals a Day. Every Qualifying Working Day.

Breakfast.

Lunch.

Dinner.

Not as charity.

Not as a replacement for wages.

Not as a marketing campaign.

But as a basic workplace-welfare benefit.

The worker keeps his salary.

The worker keeps his financial freedom.

The worker can continue supporting his family.

And at the same time, the system makes sure that the person spending the day delivering food to everyone else has access to food for himself.

Because perhaps the next evolution of the delivery industry should not only ask:

“How quickly can we get food to the customer?”

It should also ask:

“How well are we taking care of the person who brings it?”

Three meals. Every working day.
